summaries.summary: Astrophysics is the branch of astronomy that studies the physical properties, composition, and structure of celestial objects and of the universe as a whole, applying the laws of physics to understand cosmic phenomena. The Encyclopaedia Britannica characterizes it as the "branch of astronomy concerned primarily with the properties and structure of cosmic objects, including the universe as a whole." Its identity as a distinct division within astronomy is reflected in standard bibliographic classification: the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QB460-QB466 to "Astrophysics (General)" within the astronomy subclass QB. The field connects observational astronomy with theoretical physics, treating objects such as stars, galaxies, and interstellar matter as physical systems whose behavior can be modeled through the same principles that govern matter and energy on Earth.

summaries.summary: Cosmology is the study of the physical universe taken as a unified whole, including its large-scale structure, origin, and evolution. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as the "field of study that brings together the natural sciences, particularly astronomy and physics, in a joint effort to understand the physical universe as a unified whole," noting that at the largest scales a distinctive feature emerges in the form of the cosmological expansion. As a recognized division of astronomical study, it occupies its own place in standard library classification: the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QB980-QB991 the label "Cosmogony. Cosmology" within the astronomy subclass QB. The discipline draws jointly on astronomy and physics to describe phenomena that have no counterpart at smaller, local scales.

summaries.summary: Planetary science is the study of planets and other bodies of the solar system, addressing their origin, evolution, structure, and physical and chemical characteristics. NASA's planetary science program "explores the objects in our solar system to better understand its history and the distribution of life within." The field's standing as a distinct area within astronomy is reflected in standard library classification, where the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QB600-QB701 to "Planets. Planetology" and QB454-QB456 to "Astrogeology" within the astronomy subclass QB. Its scholarly community is institutionalized: the Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS), described in its own materials as "the world's largest professional society of planetary scientists," is a division of the American Astronomical Society.

summaries.summary: Geology is the study of the solid Earth — its materials, structure, processes, and history. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as comprising "the fields of study concerned with the solid Earth," noting that geology "also explores geologic history, which provides a conceptual framework and overview of Earth's evolution." Its scope spans the description of Earth materials, the processes that shape the planet, and the reconstruction of past conditions from the rock record. As a major division of the sciences, geology occupies the entire QE subclass of the Library of Congress Classification. This node represents the geological discipline as a subfield within the earth sciences, distinct from the broader earth-sciences field; its summary describes geology's own subject matter rather than the full span of the earth sciences.

summaries.summary: Geophysics applies the principles and methods of physics to the study of the Earth. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as a "major branch of the Earth sciences that applies the principles and methods of physics to the study of the Earth," dealing with a wide range of geologic phenomena. Its dual character as both an Earth science and a physics-based discipline is mirrored in standard bibliographic classification: the Library of Congress Classification places "Geophysics. Cosmic physics" at QC801-QC809, within the physics subclass QC rather than the geology subclass QE. The field uses physical observations — of gravity, magnetism, seismic wave propagation, heat, and related quantities — to infer the composition, structure, and dynamics of the Earth's interior and surface.

summaries.summary: Geochemistry is the scientific study of the chemistry of the Earth, focusing on the relative abundance, distribution, and movement of the chemical elements and their isotopes within the planet. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline that deals with the relative abundance, distribution, and migration of the Earth's chemical elements and their isotopes." The field examines how elements are partitioned among the Earth's materials and reservoirs and how they migrate through geologic processes over time. Geochemistry sits at the interface of the geological and chemical sciences, drawing on chemical analysis and theory to characterize the composition and evolution of rocks, minerals, waters, and other Earth materials.

summaries.summary: Mineralogy is the scientific study of minerals in all their aspects. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline that is concerned with all aspects of minerals, including their physical properties, chemical composition, internal crystal structure, and occurrence and distribution in nature and their origins in terms of the physicochemical conditions of formation." The field characterizes naturally occurring crystalline substances by their composition, structure, and properties, and investigates the conditions under which they form. Its identity as an established subject is reflected in standard library classification, where the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QE351-QE399.2 the label "Mineralogy" within the geology subclass QE.

summaries.summary: Petrology is the branch of geology concerned with rocks — their composition, texture, structure, occurrence, and origin. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific study of rocks that deals with their composition, texture, and structure; their occurrence and distribution; and their origin in relation to physicochemical conditions and geologic processes," and notes that it addresses all three major rock types: igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary. The field interprets rocks as records of the physical and chemical conditions under which they formed. Its standing as an established subject is reflected in standard library classification, where the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QE420-QE499 the label "Petrology" within the geology subclass QE.

summaries.summary: Paleontology is the scientific study of past life as preserved in the fossil record. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific study of life of the geologic past that involves the analysis of plant and animal fossils, including those of microscopic size, preserved in rocks," and notes that it "has played a key role in reconstructing Earth's history and has provided much evidence to support the theory of evolution." The discipline reconstructs the history of life and ancient environments from fossils ranging from microscopic remains to large organisms. Its identity as an established subject is reflected in standard library classification, where the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QE701-QE760 the label "Paleontology" within the geology subclass QE.

summaries.summary: Seismology is the study of earthquakes and of the propagation of seismic waves through the Earth. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline that is concerned with the study of earthquakes and of the propagation of seismic waves within the Earth," describing it as a branch of geophysics that has "provided much information about the composition and state of the planet's interior." The field uses recordings of seismic waves both to characterize earthquake sources and to probe the Earth's internal structure. Its scholarly community is institutionalized in bodies such as the Seismological Society of America, which presents its mission in terms of advancing "the science of seismology."

summaries.summary: Volcanology is the branch of the geologic sciences concerned with volcanoes and volcanic phenomena. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "discipline of the geologic sciences that is concerned with all aspects of volcanic phenomena," addressing "the formation, distribution, and classification of volcanoes as well as with their structure and the kinds of materials ejected during an eruption." The field studies how volcanoes form and are distributed, the products of eruptions, and the processes that drive volcanic activity. In the Library of Congress Classification, volcanoes are treated alongside earthquakes in the range QE521-QE545, labeled "Volcanoes and earthquakes," within the geology subclass QE.

summaries.summary: Atmospheric science is the study of the structure, composition, and dynamics of Earth's atmosphere. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as an "interdisciplinary field of study that combines the components of physics and chemistry that focus on the structure and dynamics of Earth's atmosphere." As an umbrella discipline, it encompasses several traditional areas; Britannica notes that "the atmospheric sciences are traditionally divided into three topical areas—meteorology (the study and forecasting of weather), climatology (the study of long-term atmospheric patterns and their influences), and aeronomy (the study of the physics and chemistry of the upper atmosphere)." The field draws on mathematical and computational tools to describe physical and chemical processes spanning timescales from hourly weather changes to long-term climate, treating meteorology and climatology as branches within its scope rather than as separate disciplines.
